CYBER TROLLS

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The consequences of cyber bulling - a phenomenon that feeds on emotional abuse in the cyber world, often with devastating consequences and very little justice.

Summary:
We live in a digital world…. Gone are the days of things like going to the library, standing in line at the bank or writing an old friend a long letter with pen and paper… with technology at our finger tips – most things take place in a cyber world… even bullying. The anonymity the internet offers, gives vindictive individuals the ability the verbally abuse and harass people without any real consequences or repercussions. Carte Blanche looks at the psychology behind this alarming new trend in emotional abuse and asks what legal protection do victims really have?



Further information:
BACKGROUND:
Bullying is no longer limited shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors… it’s gone digital… text messages, social networking and instant messaging are the latest way to torment people. The biggest frustration is that you can’t escape a cyberbully – it doesn’t end when you go home for the day... cyber bullies have access to you 24 hours a day through your phone, the internet... they don’t need to be physically in your face to harass you! Cyber bullying can be anything from spreading rumors online or via text message to posting hurtful or threatening messages on social networking sites, web pages, via email and text message to Circulating sexually suggestive pictures or messages about a person. While the initial abuse starts in a digital realm, the consequences of the abuse is real. Cyberbullies may not be in your face, but the torment still leaves a destructive trail . In some cases, the bullies have gone as far as encouraging people to commit suicide and tragically their victims have taken their own lives.

DEVASTING CONSEQUENCES At least 6 international cases of youth that have committed suicide – earlier this year a highschool boy in Welkom commited suicide after being taunted online by fellow pupils for cheating in a test.

CASE STUDY: HIGH SCHOOL PUPIL
“Amy” is 15 years old and has become the the target of her fellow learners attacks on whatsapp. They created memes of Amy comparing her laugh to that of a hyena and started sending it around the high school. “Amy” was too nervous to tell her mum for fear of retribution, so she kept the taunting a secret. Eventually of weeks of they digital onslaught, she was so traumatised by the nasty comments and vindictive attention, that Amy tried to end her life two weeks ago. Her mum found her unconscious in her room and rushed her to hospital. She has changed schools and her mom hopes that will be fresh start for her.

LIANE LURIE – PSYCHOLOGIST
Cyber-bullying is not exclusive to children and adolescents – everyone is free game when it comes this type of emotinal manipulation says Psychologist Liane Lurie – just in her practice she’s seen an influx of cyber-bullying cases and of late even more adults – she takes us through the definitions, the impacts and psychology of a cyberbully.

CASE STUDY: ADULT WOMAN
Waiting for details – ex-lover started a digital attack. She was unable to get help from the police and legally despite legislation that applies to this kind of harassment found herself frustrated, desperate and isolated.

THE CULPRITS People who have earned themselves these titles by launching tirades on the Internet, bad-mouthing anyone who comes in their way.. Cyberbullies use digital technology like the social networking, instant messaging or texting to intentionally hurt, humiliate, harass, intimidate or threaten another person. Cyber bullies target people they know in real life, in some cases not even bothering to use aliases.

BUT CAN CATCH YOU THEM? AND WHAT THEN?
Danny Myburgh is Cyber Crime Expert – he’s seen a significant spike in cyberbullying cases. The challenge is finding the true identity of the cyber bully – if you are able to trace them – getting them to back down is a whole other challenge with ineffective legislation combined with clever technology giving cyberbullies endless ways of continuing their tyriads.

Danny takes us through the challenges of catching a cyberbully.

THE LAW
Techonology Lawyer Russel Luck says while there is legislation very few cases are being tried and very little prosecutions are materialising. He’s young and funky and has a fresh take on the issues of law, social medial and technology.


HISTORY
Examples of Cyber Bullying in South Africa:
• In Springs, Gauteng, the mother of a 16- year-old girl obtained a peace order in terms of section 384 of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1955 against another 16-year-old girl at her daughter’s school. This happened after the other girl apparently regularly humiliated the woman’s daughter on MXit. The daughter’s name also appeared on a MXit ‘slut list’, which contained the names of girls from various schools in Springs, including their addresses, telephone numbers and schools. • A 16 year-old-girl from Durban tried to commit suicide after her name was put on a “slut list” that went viral on Facebook and BlackBerry Messenger. After she found her name on the list she tried to over-dose on household detergents and petrol. She recovered in hospital and was released a few days later. • A 15-year-old girl from Gauteng was harassed by four fellow pupils. They allegedly mocked her, called her fat and threw diet pills at her. They then took it further by posting nasty comments and threats on Facebook and BlackBerry Messenger. They then allegedly hit her over the head with a glass bottle, which was filmed by a fellow pupil at the attacker’s request. The assailants were suspended, returning to school a week later.

TYPES OF CYBER BULLYING
Denigration – this involves the sending or posting of cruel gossip or rumours about a person to damage his or her reputation or friendships. It often involves the spreading rumours about someone’s sexual orientation and information that is derogatory and untrue. It also includes posting or sending digitally altered photographs of someone to others, particularly pictures that portray the victim in a sexualised or harmful way. Exclusion – this is related to the designation of who is a member of the in-group and who is an outcast. The emotional impact of exclusion can be intense and may occur in an online gaming environment, group blogging environment, or any other password-protected communication environment. Flaming – this involves brief, heated online fights, where electronic messages using angry, vulgar, insulting and sometimes threatening language, are exchanged. It typically occurs in online public forums such as chat rooms, discussion groups or games. A lengthily series of these messages is called a “flame war”. Harassment – this involves frequently sending a cruel, offensive or threatening message to an individual target. This is usually done via a person’s e-mail account, mobile phone or other personal communication channel. It may cause alarm, annoyance or emotional stress to the receiver. The South African Law Reform Commission distinguishes between direct and indirect online harassment. Direct harassment includes threats, bullying or intimidating electronic messages sent directly to the victim. Indirect harassment includes spreading rumours about the victim on internet discussion forums, subscribing the victim to unwanted online services and posting information about the victim on online dating or sex services. Outing or trickery – this involves sharing someone’s secrets or embarrassing information or images online with people whom the information was never intended to be shared. In some instances deception is used to trick someone into revealing their secrets or embarrassing information, and these are then shared online with others. Happy slapping – a relatively new type of cyber bullying – involves incidents where people walk up to someone and slap them, while another captures the violence using a camera phone or digital camera. In some cases it constitutes more than slapping and assault may ensue

Press Release:


Cyber Bullying
Gone are the days of going to the library, standing in a line at the bank or writing an old friend a letter with pen and paper. With technology at our finger tips, we live and operate in a cyber world. But the anonymity the internet offers gives vindictive individuals the ability to verbally abuse and harass others without any real consequences or repercussions. Carte Blanche looks at the psychology behind this alarming trend in emotional abuse and asks what legal protection victims really have against cyber bullies?


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: The Digital world has given rise to a new breed of bully, far more dangerous than the old school thug.

LINK: This is the playground of the cyberbully, there are no merry-go-rounds – there are no swings and no slides, but there’s an endless possibility to do harm.

LIANE: cyber bullying is relentless, it is 24/7, and for the victim there is no escape, they don’t know when it’s going strike and very, very often their perpetrator is faceless

VO: Bullying is no longer limited to a shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors - it’s gone digital. Victims are tormented using text messages and social networking platforms – in the digital realm, everyone is susceptible.

15 year old Thembi became the target of vindictive pupils at her high school this year.

THEMBI: There was a group of matrics, that it doesn’t mean that because I am light in complexion that I am beautiful, they said, not all yellowbones are beautiful, here’s an example.

VO: But they took it a step further and created this meme.

THEMBI: they started comparing me to a hyena, saying my mouth looked like a hyena.
BONGANI: How many people had seen the pictures
THEMBI: Firstly they would send it to everyone around the school and then people from school would laugh about it and send it to other people at different schools, and then when everybody had it they will start posting it on facebook.

VO: Cyber Crime Expert Danny Myburgh says when it comes to bullying, the cyber world is much scarier than the bricks and mortar one.

DANNY: In the old days when a bully intimidated a person, it would only be the ring of people around them that was aware of it, but now what is happening it’s been retweeted, it’s been liked, it’s been shared, so literally it could have been 20 people that knew about it, now millions of people would maybe know your face.

BONGANI: how did it make you feel when they were passing these pictures?
THEMBI: It’s very painful, and it’s very heartbreaking when you know that everyone is actually against you at school for some weird reason, you don’t know really why and there’s nothing you can do about it.

VO: The abuse is real says Clinical Psychologist Liane Lurie.

LIANE: Individual experience has a sense of torment, // the world as they knew it, the safe place that they envisioned for themselves has been exceptionally disrupted,// experience huge level of anxiety , thoughts of self-harm, major levels of depression,

VO: Thembi hoped that the nasty comments would eventually stop, but what started out as a big laugh would eventually push her to attempt suicide.

THEMBI: I took three pills, nothing happened, and I took three more pills, and then I was like 6 is not enough, and I took more pills.... I thought I was going to die, and then I don't have to face anything at school.
BONGANI: Weren’t you scared that you might die
THEMBI: I was...// what if I sleep and I never wake up, then what? But there was nothing I could do about it, I already drank the pills.

VO: Thembi was rushed to hospital – after receiving treatment, she was discharged and has been moved to a new school.

LINK: it comes in various guises, from flaming to trolling and others, but the trail of destruction is the same - it makes like almost unbearable for it’s targets.

VO: Attacks are not limited to youngsters, adults who work and play in the digital world are just as vulnerable.

Lynsay Young started getting emails from unknown address in November 2012, soon after she started dating her now husband, Roland.

LYNSAY: I received an email what a dreadful boyfriend I had, he was having affairs, he was a conartist, he would sponge off me, terrible things.

VO: This cyber-bully targeted her friends, family and colleagues using different aliases to spread awful rumours.

LYNSAY: Her latest stunt was placing now, my ex-husband on a dating website and then she emailed me to say look you’re husband is now not interested in you any more, he’s now very bored of you, he’s now looking for other women.
LIANE: For the cyberbully they also derive some kind of power, pleasure and gratification from the pain that they are inflicting.

BONGANI: Do you have any idea who it is?
LYNSAY: Three years later I don’t know

LINK: The harassment, the humiliation and the hurt caused by cyberbullies is real, it’s almost impossible to catch an invisible tormentor. INVISIBLE LINK

VO: Culprits hide behind screens using fake profiles to torment by technology.

BONGANI: It seems like these guys are winning?
DANNY: Unfortunately it is very difficult for us to investigate it, the success rate is low, //it could be a time consuming investigation and it could be costly, so a person really needs to make that decision, where it is worth their while to have it investigated

VO: Cyber stealth programmes, allow bullies to disappear into the code.

DANNY: you can go in and everything that you do then your identity is scrubbed, it means it is removed, very little of your identity is traceable from there.

VO: With this anonymity, cyber attacks often gain momentum as this breed of bully believes they are untouchable.

SARAH: There is just always this one thing at the back of your head, so you can never be fully comfortable, and for a while I was scared of social media, I was scared to put a photo up in case this person would comment

VO: Sarah is an up and coming online media presenter who has become the target of a faceless hater, who started off insulting her appearance and weight, and alleged that she was unfaithful to her boyfriend.

SARAH: You don’t fully understand what’s happening to you. // I’m not in high school anymore, I’m 23 years old, I finished studying I’ve got my first job, I’m excited, you don’t expect to have that kind of bullying and drama // as an adult to have it as well.

VO: Liane says this, is the coward’s way of bullying - vengeful from a distance.

LIANE: it’s that’s much easier to perpetrate, there is a disconnect between them and their victim, they don’t see the impact that they are having on the victim.

VO: Sarah knew it was serious when they started targeting her work.

SARAH: They would tweet my work, saying I’m rubbish at my job, the should bring back the old person, and it started getting progressively worse and it made me fearful that, you know, I mean it’s embarrassing for me to explain to my work, listen I’m sorry I have a cyber-bully.

VO: These attackers hide behind screens and are tech-savvy individuals, who know their way around cyber space says Danny.

DANNY: People that have a lot of knowledge regarding social media and the mechanisms that is available, so if these types of platforms are unknown to you, you’re not going to make a very good perpetrator in this environment.

VO: But just what is the responsibility of social media platforms?

DANNY: proactively, no requirement on them, but all of them do have the facility where you can report abuse or where you can report activity like this, and after you have reported it to them, there is legal steps you can take against the platform if they do not remove that information.

VO: Liane believes individuals perpatrators are to blame.

LIANE: Guns don’t kill people, people kill people. So yes, social media and it’s an ever evolving phenomenon certainly contribute but you are the one at the end of the day that manipulates the photo.

VO: Bringing the culprits to book, can be tricky says Techonology Lawyer Russel Luck.

RUSSEL: The big problem with this area of law is that it is very new, // Cyberbullying is a concept that covers many different activities, yes it is a crime under a serious scale where it amounts to hate speech or harassment, on the lesser scale when it amounts to defamation then it becomes a civil wrong.

VO: Although it could result in a fine or even jail time, Lindsay says despite having her suspicions about who it could be, she’s not getting help from authorities

LYNSAY: I think it’s an ex, but with no proof, we’re at a standstill. Attorneys can’t help, investigators can’t help, the police aren’t interested at all.

VO: As signatories of Budapest convention pertaining to cyber crime, SA is up to date with the latest international trends in cyber crime and cyber law

RUSSEL: SA like all other countries in the world has extended the normal rights that a person has to their dignity and their personality in the digital realm. SA is always a case of excellent laws with the challenge of enforcement // when you are dealing with a plethora of rapes and murders and other crimes of that nature it’s very difficult to kind of enforce the laws effectivelyI

VO: But Danny say this shouldn’t deter victims from reporting these cases and taking investigations further.

DANNY: , what we see a lot of times though is that if a person targets a victim, they will continue to do so, the more they target the person, the more the activity increases, the better our chances are that that person will slip up. //

VO: Keep a record of the all the attacks, the comments and the pictures to help build your case says Russel.

BONGANI: most people want to delete it
RUSsEL Essentially you are deleting evidence.

VO: But even with the evidence, victims like Sarah are still in the dark.

SARAH: the main question is why? //What could I have done that was so great for them to go on for over a year. // That’s tough to think about because you start to question yourself., the hardest think I was also questioning my friends, not knowing who to trust.

LIANE: i think it fills them with a tremendous amount of trepidation// they have that sort of fight or flight response, because they don’t know what actually is coming next, they are not able to defend themselves appropriately,

LYNSAY: you actually want to hide away so that she can hopefully forget about you, but it’s not happening - for her it’s a game, not for us.




PROMOS

PROMO 1 – 10 seconds
VO: From school ground taunts to torment by technology – the new face of bullying.

LIANE: cyber bullying is relentless, it is 24/7, and for the victim there is no escape,

PROMO 2 – 15 seconds
VO: Bullies hide behind screens to launch vindictive attacks in the digital realm - everyone is susceptible and no one can escape.

SARAH: I’m not in high school anymore, I’m 23 years old, you don’t expect to have that kind of bullying and drama.

PROMO 3 – 15 seconds
VO: While invisible cyber bullies attack in the digital realm, the impact is real, and can have devastating consequences for it’s victims

THEMBI: I took more pills.... I thought I was going to die, and then I don't have to face anything at school.

Carte Blanche looks at the psychology behind this alarming trend in emotional abuse and asks what legal protection victims really have against cyber bullies? Script: STRUCTURE VO: The Digital world has given rise to a new breed of bully, far more dangerous than the old school thug. LINK: This is the playground of the cyberbully, there are no merry-go-rounds – there are no swings and no slides, but there’s an endless possibility to do harm. LIANE: cyber bullying is relentless, it is 24/7, and for the victim there is no escape, they don’t know when it’s going strike and very, very often their perpetrator is faceless VO: Bullying is no longer limited to a shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors - it’s gone digital. Victims are tormented using text messages and social networking platforms – in the digital realm, everyone is susceptible. 15 year old Thembi became the target of vindictive pupils at her high school this year. THEMBI: There was a group of matrics, that it doesn’t mean that because I am light in complexion that I am beautiful, they said, not all yellowbones are beautiful, here’s an example. VO: But they took it a step further and created this meme. THEMBI: they started comparing me to a hyena, saying my mouth looked like a hyena. BONGANI: How many people had seen the pictures THEMBI: Firstly they would send it to everyone around the school and then people from school would laugh about it and send it to other people at different schools, and then when everybody had it they will start posting it on facebook. VO: Cyber Crime Expert Danny Myburgh says when it comes to bullying, the cyber world is much scarier than the bricks and mortar one. DANNY: In the old days when a bully intimidated a person, it would only be the ring of people around them that was aware of it, but now what is happening it’s been retweeted, it’s been liked, it’s been shared, so literally it could have been 20 people that knew about it, now millions of people would maybe know your face. BONGANI: how did it make you feel when they were passing these pictures? THEMBI: It’s very painful, and it’s very heartbreaking when you know that everyone is actually against you at school for some weird reason, you don’t know really why and there’s nothing you can do about it. VO: The abuse is real says Clinical Psychologist Liane Lurie. LIANE: Individual experience has a sense of torment, // the world as they knew it, the safe place that they envisioned for themselves has been exceptionally disrupted,// experience huge level of anxiety , thoughts of self-harm, major levels of depression, VO: Thembi hoped that the nasty comments would eventually stop, but what started out as a big laugh would eventually push her to attempt suicide. THEMBI: I took three pills, nothing happened, and I took three more pills, and then I was like 6 is not enough, and I took more pills.... I thought I was going to die, and then I don't have to face anything at school. BONGANI: Weren’t you scared that you might die THEMBI: I was...// what if I sleep and I never wake up, then what? But there was nothing I could do about it, I already drank the pills. VO: Thembi was rushed to hospital – after receiving treatment, she was discharged and has been moved to a new school. LINK: it comes in various guises, from flaming to trolling and others, but the trail of destruction is the same - it makes like almost unbearable for it’s targets. VO: Attacks are not limited to youngsters, adults who work and play in the digital world are just as vulnerable. Lynsay Young started getting emails from unknown address in November 2012, soon after she started dating her now husband, Roland. LYNSAY: I received an email what a dreadful boyfriend I had, he was having affairs, he was a conartist, he would sponge off me, terrible things. VO: This cyber-bully targeted her friends, family and colleagues using different aliases to spread awful rumours. LYNSAY: Her latest stunt was placing now, my ex-husband on a dating website and then she emailed me to say look you’re husband is now not interested in you any more, he’s now very bored of you, he’s now looking for other women. LIANE: For the cyberbully they also derive some kind of power, pleasure and gratification from the pain that they are inflicting. BONGANI: Do you have any idea who it is? LYNSAY: Three years later I don’t know LINK: The harassment, the humiliation and the hurt caused by cyberbullies is real, it’s almost impossible to catch an invisible tormentor. INVISIBLE LINK VO: Culprits hide behind screens using fake profiles to torment by technology. BONGANI: It seems like these guys are winning? DANNY: Unfortunately it is very difficult for us to investigate it, the success rate is low, //it could be a time consuming investigation and it could be costly, so a person really needs to make that decision, where it is worth their while to have it investigated VO: Cyber stealth programmes, allow bullies to disappear into the code. DANNY: you can go in and everything that you do then your identity is scrubbed, it means it is removed, very little of your identity is traceable from there. VO: With this anonymity, cyber attacks often gain momentum as this breed of bully believes they are untouchable. SARAH: There is just always this one thing at the back of your head, so you can never be fully comfortable, and for a while I was scared of social media, I was scared to put a photo up in case this person would comment VO: Sarah is an up and coming online media presenter who has become the target of a faceless hater, who started off insulting her appearance and weight, and alleged that she was unfaithful to her boyfriend. SARAH: You don’t fully understand what’s happening to you. // I’m not in high school anymore, I’m 23 years old, I finished studying I’ve got my first job, I’m excited, you don’t expect to have that kind of bullying and drama // as an adult to have it as well. VO: Liane says this, is the coward’s way of bullying - vengeful from a distance. LIANE: it’s that’s much easier to perpetrate, there is a disconnect between them and their victim, they don’t see the impact that they are having on the victim. VO: Sarah knew it was serious when they started targeting her work. SARAH: They would tweet my work, saying I’m rubbish at my job, the should bring back the old person, and it started getting progressively worse and it made me fearful that, you know, I mean it’s embarrassing for me to explain to my work, listen I’m sorry I have a cyber-bully. VO: These attackers hide behind screens and are tech-savvy individuals, who know their way around cyber space says Danny. DANNY: People that have a lot of knowledge regarding social media and the mechanisms that is available, so if these types of platforms are unknown to you, you’re not going to make a very good perpetrator in this environment. VO: But just what is the responsibility of social media platforms? DANNY: proactively, no requirement on them, but all of them do have the facility where you can report abuse or where you can report activity like this, and after you have reported it to them, there is legal steps you can take against the platform if they do not remove that information. VO: Liane believes individuals perpatrators are to blame. LIANE: Guns don’t kill people, people kill people. So yes, social media and it’s an ever evolving phenomenon certainly contribute but you are the one at the end of the day that manipulates the photo. VO: Bringing the culprits to book, can be tricky says Techonology Lawyer Russel Luck. RUSSEL: The big problem with this area of law is that it is very new, // Cyberbullying is a concept that covers many different activities, yes it is a crime under a serious scale where it amounts to hate speech or harassment, on the lesser scale when it amounts to defamation then it becomes a civil wrong. VO: Although it could result in a fine or even jail time, Lindsay says despite having her suspicions about who it could be, she’s not getting help from authorities LYNSAY: I think it’s an ex, but with no proof, we’re at a standstill. Attorneys can’t help, investigators can’t help, the police aren’t interested at all. VO: As signatories of Budapest convention pertaining to cyber crime, SA is up to date with the latest international trends in cyber crime and cyber law RUSSEL: SA like all other countries in the world has extended the normal rights that a person has to their dignity and their personality in the digital realm. SA is always a case of excellent laws with the challenge of enforcement // when you are dealing with a plethora of rapes and murders and other crimes of that nature it’s very difficult to kind of enforce the laws effectivelyI VO: But Danny say this shouldn’t deter victims from reporting these cases and taking investigations further. DANNY: , what we see a lot of times though is that if a person targets a victim, they will continue to do so, the more they target the person, the more the activity increases, the better our chances are that that person will slip up. // VO: Keep a record of the all the attacks, the comments and the pictures to help build your case says Russel. BONGANI: most people want to delete it RUSsEL Essentially you are deleting evidence. VO: But even with the evidence, victims like Sarah are still in the dark. SARAH: the main question is why? //What could I have done that was so great for them to go on for over a year. // That’s tough to think about because you start to question yourself., the hardest think I was also questioning my friends, not knowing who to trust. LIANE: i think it fills them with a tremendous amount of trepidation// they have that sort of fight or flight response, because they don’t know what actually is coming next, they are not able to defend themselves appropriately, LYNSAY: you actually want to hide away so that she can hopefully forget about you, but it’s not happening - for her it’s a game, not for us. PROMOS PROMO 1 – 10 seconds VO: From school ground taunts to torment by technology – the new face of bullying. LIANE: cyber bullying is relentless, it is 24/7, and for the victim there is no escape, PROMO 2 – 15 seconds VO: Bullies hide behind screens to launch vindictive attacks in the digital realm - everyone is susceptible and no one can escape. SARAH: I’m not in high school anymore, I’m 23 years old, you don’t expect to have that kind of bullying and drama. PROMO 3 – 15 seconds VO: While invisible cyber bullies attack in the digital realm, the impact is real, and can have devastating consequences for it’s victims THEMBI: I took more pills.... I thought I was going to die, and then I don't have to face anything at school. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The consequences of cyber bulling - a phenomenon that feeds on emotional abuse in the cyber world, often with devastating consequences and very little justice.
metadata.Summary: We live in a digital world…. Gone are the days of things like going to the library, standing in line at the bank or writing an old friend a long letter with pen and paper… with technology at our finger tips – most things take place in a cyber world… even bullying. The anonymity the internet offers, gives vindictive individuals the ability the verbally abuse and harass people without any real consequences or repercussions. Carte Blanche looks at the psychology behind this alarming new trend in emotional abuse and asks what legal protection do victims really have?
metadata.Further information: BACKGROUND: Bullying is no longer limited shove on the playground or random taunts in school corridors… it’s gone digital… text messages, social networking and instant messaging are the latest way to torment people. The biggest frustration is that you can’t escape a cyberbully – it doesn’t end when you go home for the day... cyber bullies have access to you 24 hours a day through your phone, the internet... they don’t need to be physically in your face to harass you! Cyber bullying can be anything from spreading rumors online or via text message to posting hurtful or threatening messages on social networking sites, web pages, via email and text message to Circulating sexually suggestive pictures or messages about a person. While the initial abuse starts in a digital realm, the consequences of the abuse is real. Cyberbullies may not be in your face, but the torment still leaves a destructive trail . In some cases, the bullies have gone as far as encouraging people to commit suicide and tragically their victims have taken their own lives. DEVASTING CONSEQUENCES At least 6 international cases of youth that have committed suicide – earlier this year a highschool boy in Welkom commited suicide after being taunted online by fellow pupils for cheating in a test. CASE STUDY: HIGH SCHOOL PUPIL “Amy” is 15 years old and has become the the target of her fellow learners attacks on whatsapp. They created memes of Amy comparing her laugh to that of a hyena and started sending it around the high school. “Amy” was too nervous to tell her mum for fear of retribution, so she kept the taunting a secret. Eventually of weeks of they digital onslaught, she was so traumatised by the nasty comments and vindictive attention, that Amy tried to end her life two weeks ago. Her mum found her unconscious in her room and rushed her to hospital. She has changed schools and her mom hopes that will be fresh start for her. LIANE LURIE – PSYCHOLOGIST Cyber-bullying is not exclusive to children and adolescents – everyone is free game when it comes this type of emotinal manipulation says Psychologist Liane Lurie – just in her practice she’s seen an influx of cyber-bullying cases and of late even more adults – she takes us through the definitions, the impacts and psychology of a cyberbully. CASE STUDY: ADULT WOMAN Waiting for details – ex-lover started a digital attack. She was unable to get help from the police and legally despite legislation that applies to this kind of harassment found herself frustrated, desperate and isolated. THE CULPRITS People who have earned themselves these titles by launching tirades on the Internet, bad-mouthing anyone who comes in their way.. Cyberbullies use digital technology like the social networking, instant messaging or texting to intentionally hurt, humiliate, harass, intimidate or threaten another person. Cyber bullies target people they know in real life, in some cases not even bothering to use aliases. BUT CAN CATCH YOU THEM? AND WHAT THEN? Danny Myburgh is Cyber Crime Expert – he’s seen a significant spike in cyberbullying cases. The challenge is finding the true identity of the cyber bully – if you are able to trace them – getting them to back down is a whole other challenge with ineffective legislation combined with clever technology giving cyberbullies endless ways of continuing their tyriads. Danny takes us through the challenges of catching a cyberbully. THE LAW Techonology Lawyer Russel Luck says while there is legislation very few cases are being tried and very little prosecutions are materialising. He’s young and funky and has a fresh take on the issues of law, social medial and technology. HISTORY Examples of Cyber Bullying in South Africa: • In Springs, Gauteng, the mother of a 16- year-old girl obtained a peace order in terms of section 384 of the Criminal Procedure Act, 1955 against another 16-year-old girl at her daughter’s school. This happened after the other girl apparently regularly humiliated the woman’s daughter on MXit. The daughter’s name also appeared on a MXit ‘slut list’, which contained the names of girls from various schools in Springs, including their addresses, telephone numbers and schools. • A 16 year-old-girl from Durban tried to commit suicide after her name was put on a “slut list” that went viral on Facebook and BlackBerry Messenger. After she found her name on the list she tried to over-dose on household detergents and petrol. She recovered in hospital and was released a few days later. • A 15-year-old girl from Gauteng was harassed by four fellow pupils. They allegedly mocked her, called her fat and threw diet pills at her. They then took it further by posting nasty comments and threats on Facebook and BlackBerry Messenger. They then allegedly hit her over the head with a glass bottle, which was filmed by a fellow pupil at the attacker’s request. The assailants were suspended, returning to school a week later. TYPES OF CYBER BULLYING Denigration – this involves the sending or posting of cruel gossip or rumours about a person to damage his or her reputation or friendships. It often involves the spreading rumours about someone’s sexual orientation and information that is derogatory and untrue. It also includes posting or sending digitally altered photographs of someone to others, particularly pictures that portray the victim in a sexualised or harmful way. Exclusion – this is related to the designation of who is a member of the in-group and who is an outcast. The emotional impact of exclusion can be intense and may occur in an online gaming environment, group blogging environment, or any other password-protected communication environment. Flaming – this involves brief, heated online fights, where electronic messages using angry, vulgar, insulting and sometimes threatening language, are exchanged. It typically occurs in online public forums such as chat rooms, discussion groups or games. A lengthily series of these messages is called a “flame war”. Harassment – this involves frequently sending a cruel, offensive or threatening message to an individual target. This is usually done via a person’s e-mail account, mobile phone or other personal communication channel. It may cause alarm, annoyance or emotional stress to the receiver. The South African Law Reform Commission distinguishes between direct and indirect online harassment. Direct harassment includes threats, bullying or intimidating electronic messages sent directly to the victim. Indirect harassment includes spreading rumours about the victim on internet discussion forums, subscribing the victim to unwanted online services and posting information about the victim on online dating or sex services. Outing or trickery – this involves sharing someone’s secrets or embarrassing information or images online with people whom the information was never intended to be shared. In some instances deception is used to trick someone into revealing their secrets or embarrassing information, and these are then shared online with others. Happy slapping – a relatively new type of cyber bullying – involves incidents where people walk up to someone and slap them, while another captures the violence using a camera phone or digital camera. In some cases it constitutes more than slapping and assault may ensue
